newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pro-Karadzic rally mirrors Bosnia election woes.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Karadzic rally mirrors Bosnia election woes.

text.p: International organisers of Bosnia's elections said on Friday that Serbs were trampling on campaign rules by lionising indicted war criminals, but no counter-measures were immediately in the offing.

The OSCE's strong words, but hesitancy to act, underlined the fading promise of the September 14 vote which is supposed to reunify Bosnia but has been all but hijacked by nationalist factions bent on ratifying its wartime division.

Serbs at an election rally outside Sarajevo on Thursday waved posters of separatist Serb army commander General Ratko Mladic and wartime political leader Radovan Karadzic, and speakers repeatedly praised the two men.

As indictees of a U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia, Karadzic and Mladic are banned from political activity in Bosnia under the 1995 Dayton peace treaty. Their images may not be displayed or evoked in public.

But the ban, meant to bolster the credibility of the voting for governing bodies to reintegrate the three nationalist sectors of Bosnia, has been flouted in Serb Republic territory with impunity, independent monitors say.

Some speakers at the Serb Democratic Party rally, including Serb Republic officials, shouted "Long Live President Karadzic" although he formally quit politics in July to save the SDS from being disqualified from the election.

Officials of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which is organising the elections, agreed the rally ignored campaign rules but said a decision on action, if any, would not be taken until Tuesday.

"We have reports that the most egregious incidents took place at the rally yesterday...but we don't have enforcement (powers) on the ground," Agota Kuperman, OSCE spokeswoman in Bosnia, told a news conference.

The Party of Democratic Action (SDA), which rules mainly Moslem parts of Bosnia, filed a protest over the SDS rally with the OSCE. The SDA is fielding candidates throughout the Moslem-Croat federation, but is also running for office in Serb Republic towns from which Moslems were expelled in wartime.

Kuperman said Robert Frowick, the ex-U.S. diplomat heading the OSCE mission in Bosnia, sent the official in charge of the OSCE's election appeals board to the Serb capital Pale to "gather evidence" and rebuke the Serbs.
"Ambassador Frowick is concerned at reports of such constant, repetitive (behaviour) on the part of the SDS. We are now moving as expeditiously as possible," she said.
The OSCE is empowered to bar candidates or an entire party from the elections for grave violations of campaign rules, including involvement or influence of war-crimes indictees.
But observers expected the OSCE to do little for fear of seeing the SDS sabotage voting in its domain through its control of the police and local election committees.
"Frowick will consult with lots of people now to think of ways to save the elections without looking weak," said a Western humanitarian official who asked not to be named.
"But he cannot strike the SDS off the ballot list or the elections would go bust on Serb territory (half of Bosnia) and then he wipes out his raison d'etre," the official said.
The U.S.-engineered Dayton treaty explicitly requires the elections to be "free and fair" but human rights monitors say conditions for a democratic vote are non-existent in Bosnia.
The three ruling nationalist parties have stifled free speech and free movement while orchestrating bombings and mob violence against moderate opposition rivals.

Critics say Dayton set an arbitrary early deadline of September 1996 for elections to pave the way for a NATO peace force withdrawal within a year of the treaty, which would help U.S. President Bill Clinton win re-election this November.

Kuperman denied reports that OSCE was trying to sideline the chief of independent election monitors Ed van Thijn in case he challenges the validity of the outcome after having branded the pre-election process "a fraud".
"There is no truth to insinuations that his mandate is to be changed in any way," she said.
